'''William Clyde Martin Jr.''' (November 27, 1929 &ndash; September 15, 2013) was an American [[physicist]]. After receiving his Ph.D. degree from Princeton University in 1956, he joined the staff of the [[National Institute of Standards and Technology|National Bureau of Standards]] (NBS: now NIST, the National Institute of Standards and Technology), where he was employed until his retirement in 1998.  As Chief of the NBS [[Atomic spectroscopy|Atomic Spectroscopy]] Section (and its successor organizations) from 1962 to 1998, he led the development of its reference data resources on the spectra of rare-earth elements, substantially increased its coverage of highly excited and ionized species, and pioneered the publication of NIST Standard Reference Data on the internet.

==Life==
Martin was in born in [[Cullman, Alabama]] on November 27, 1929. He received a B.S. in physics from the [[University of Richmond]] in 1951 and then pursued graduate studies at [[Princeton University]], where he received a [[Doctor of Philosophy|Ph.D.]] in physics after completing a doctoral dissertation, titled "The energy levels and spectra of neutral and singly ionized [[phosphorus]]", under the supervision of [[Allen Shenstone|Allen G. Shenstone]].<ref>{{Cite book|last=Martin|first=W. C.|url=https://catalog.princeton.edu/catalog/2795219|title=The energy levels and spectra of neutral and singly ionized phosphorus|date=1956|language=English}}</ref> As a student at Princeton, he had some encounters with [[Albert Einstein]], who lived near his lodgings. Martin served as an instructor in physics at Princeton during 1955–1957. In 1957 he was hired as a physicist by the [[National Institute of Standards and Technology|National Bureau of Standards]], where he spent the rest of his career, retiring in 1998 and remaining active as an emeritus member of staff until his death in 2013.

In 1959 he married Dolores Moyano. They had two sons, Eric B. Martin and Christian B. Martin.

==Scientific contributions==
In 1962, Martin was appointed chief of the [[National Institute of Standards and Technology|NBS]] Atomic Spectroscopy Section (later renamed the Atomic Spectroscopy Group), and his most influential work was done in that capacity and during his subsequent leadership of its successor organizations until 1998.

The generation, curation and publication of critically evaluated data on atomic energy levels was a major scientific activity of NBS when Martin joined its staff.

That program had resulted in the publication of three landmark monographs<ref>{{cite book|author=Moore, Charlotte E.|year=1949 |title=Atomic energy levels as derived from the analyses of optical spectra|volume=1|location=[[Washington, D.C.]]|publisher=[[U.S. Government Printing Office]]}}</ref><ref>{{cite book|author=Moore, Charlotte E.|year=1952|title=Atomic energy levels as derived from the analyses of optical spectra|volume=2|location=Washington, D.C.|publisher=U.S. Government Printing Office}}</ref><ref>{{cite book|author=Moore, Charlotte E.|year=1958|title=Atomic energy levels as derived from the analyses of optical spectra|volume=3|location=Washington, D.C.|publisher=U.S. Government Printing Office}}</ref> Widely known in the spectroscopy community as ''Charlotte Moore's tables'', these monographs, which have been cited over 10,000 times in the scientific literature, tabulated the energies and other properties of atomic energy levels of the elements from [[hydrogen]] ([[atomic number]] ''Z'' = 1) through [[actinium]] ([[atomic number]] ''Z'' = 89), except for the rare-earth elements, [[cerium]] ([[atomic number]] ''Z'' = 58) through [[lutetium]] ([[atomic number]] ''Z'' = 71).

Martin began a long project of analysis of the spectra of the rare earths that resulted in numerous research publications and a fourth monograph,<ref>{{cite book|author=Martin, W. C.|author2=Zalubas, Romuald|author3=Hagan, Lucy|year=1978|title=Atomic energy levels - The rare-earth elements|location=[[Washington, D.C.]]|publisher=[[U.S. Government Printing Office]]|bibcode=1978aelr.book.....M}}</ref>
that completed the NBS coverage of the periodic table up to the actinide series. In 1963, he established<ref>{{cite journal|author=Martin, W. C.|year=1963|title=Low Energy Levels of Neutral Cerium (Ce I)|journal=J. Opt. Soc. Am.|volume=5|issue=9|page=1047|doi=10.1364/JOSA.53.001047|bibcode=1963JOSA...53.1047M}}</ref> that the ground level of atomic [[cerium]] is of the form 6''s''<sup>2</sup>5''d''4''f'' <sup>1</sup>G<sub>4</sub>°, in standard notation.<ref>
{{cite book|author=Martin, W. C.|author2=Wiese, W. L.|editor=Drake, G. W. F.|title=Springer Handbook of Atomic, Molecular and Optical Physics|publisher=Springer|year=2006|pages=175–198 |chapter=Chapter 10: Atomic Spectroscopy|isbn=978-0-387-20802-2|chapter-url=https://www.nist.gov/pml/pubs/atspec/index.cfm}}
</ref>
At the time, it was widely believed that the ground electronic configuration of this element was 6''s''<sup>2</sup>4''f''<sup>2</sup>, an error that could still be found in reference sources fifty years later.<ref>{{cite web|title=cerium (Ce)|publisher=[[Encyclopædia Britannica]]|date=2012-10-02|url=http://www.britannica.com/EBchecked/topic/103535/cerium-Ce|accessdate=2014-01-08}}</ref>

In the 1970s and 1980s, basic scientific advances, such as laser and plasma spectroscopy, and user needs, particularly those of the nuclear fusion and astrophysics communities, were generating vast quantities of new atomic spectral data and additional data needs, notably those associated with highly excited or ionized species. Martin and his co-workers initiated analyses that covered data from all ions of most second-row elements in the periodic table:

*[[sodium]].<ref>{{cite journal|author=Martin, W. C.|author2=Zalubas, Romuald|year=1981|title=Energy levels of Sodium, Na I through Na XI|journal=J. Phys. Chem. Ref. Data|volume=10|issue=1|page=153|doi=10.1063/1.555637|bibcode=1981JPCRD..10..153M|s2cid=96405107}}</ref> 
*[[magnesium]].<ref>{{cite journal|author=Martin, W. C.|author2=Zalubas, Romuald|year=1980|title=Energy levels of Magnesium, Mg I through Mg XII|journal= J. Phys. Chem. Ref. Data|volume=9|issue=1|page=1|doi=10.1063/1.555617|bibcode=1980JPCRD...9....1M|s2cid=95690896}}</ref>
*[[aluminum]].<ref>{{cite journal|author1=Martin, W. C.|author2=Zalubas, Romuald|year=1979|title=Energy levels of Aluminum, Al I through Al XIII|journal=J. Phys. Chem. Ref. Data|volume=8|issue=3|page=817|doi=10.1063/1.555608|bibcode=1979JPCRD...8..817M|s2cid=96058180}}</ref>
*[[silicon]].<ref>{{cite journal|author=Martin, W. C.|author2=Zalubas, Romuald|year=1983|title=Energy levels of Silicon, Si I through Si XIV|journal=J. Phys. Chem. Ref. Data|volume=12|issue=2|page=323|doi=10.1063/1.555685|bibcode=1983JPCRD..12..323M}}</ref>
*[[phosphorus]].<ref>{{cite journal|author=Martin, W. C.|author2=Zalubas, Romuald|year=1985|title=Energy levels of Phosphorus, P I through P XV|journal= J. Phys. Chem. Ref. Data|volume=14|issue=3|page=751|doi=10.1063/1.555736|author3=Musgrove, Arlene|bibcode=1985JPCRD..14..751M|s2cid=95776698}}</ref>
*[[sulfur]].<ref>{{cite journal|author=Martin, W. C.|author2=Zalubas, Romuald|author3=Musgrove, Arlene|year=1990|title= Energy levels of Sulfur, S I through S XVI|journal=J. Phys. Chem. Ref. Data|volume=19|issue=4|page=821|doi=10.1063/1.555862|bibcode=1990JPCRD..19..821M}}</ref>

The culminating effort of this period was a major atomic spectral compilation,<ref>{{cite journal|author=Sugar, Jack|author2=Corliss, Charles|year=1985|title=Atomic Energy Levels of the Iron-Period Elements: Potassium through Nickel|url=https://www.nist.gov/data/PDFfiles/jpcrdS2Vol14.pdf|journal=J. Phys. Chem. Ref. Data|at='''14''', Supp. 2, pp. 1 - 664|bibcode=1985aeli.book.....S|archive-date=2016-03-04|access-date=2017-07-13|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160304003516/http://www.nist.gov/data/PDFfiles/jpcrdS2Vol14.pdf|url-status=dead}}</ref> issued in print by NBS in 1985 under Martin's supervision: a 664-page compilation of all data known then, for all ionization stages of the elements potassium ([[atomic number]] ''Z'' = 19) through [[nickel]] ([[atomic number]] ''Z'' = 28).

At that time it was clear that the vast expansion of atomic data could no longer be adequately disseminated by print publications alone. Many NIST data publications had been converted to magnetic storage media, which could be purchased from the NIST Standard Reference Data Program. In the early 1990s, perceiving the potential of the [[World Wide Web]], Martin persuaded NIST management to allow free distribution of NIST atomic data on the internet. This was the first foray of NIST into free online data distribution, which remains in place today and has since been followed by other NIST data resources.

The most comprehensive of the NIST atomic data products is the ''NIST Atomic Spectra Database'' (ASD).<ref>{{cite web|title=Atomic Spectra Database|publisher=[[National Institute of Standards and Technology]]|date=March 1995|url=https://www.nist.gov/pml/data/asd.cfm|accessdate=2014-01-02}}</ref> First placed online in March, 1995, it was serving about 60,000 page requests per month in late 2013. In addition to his many contributions to ASD, Martin was coauthor of ''The Handbook of Basic Atomic Spectroscopic Data'',<ref>{{cite web|author=Sansonetti, J. E.|author2=Martin, W. C.|title=The Handbook of Basic Atomic Spectroscopic Data|publisher=National Institute of Standards and Technology|date=March 2003|url=http://nist.gov/pml/data/handbook/index.cfm|accessdate=2014-01-02}}</ref> which contains data on spectra of neutral atoms and singly charged ions of all elements from [[hydrogen]] through [[einsteinium]] ([[atomic number]] ''Z'' = 99).  He was also the architect of the NIST ''Periodic Table: Atomic Properties of the Elements'',<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.nist.gov/pml/data/periodic.cfm|title=Periodic Table: Atomic Properties of the Elements|author=Dragoset, R. A.|author2=Musgrove, A.|author3=Clark, C. W.|author4=Martin, W. C.|series=NIST Special Publication 966|publisher=National Institute of Standards and Technology|accessdate=2014-01-07|date=2009-07-30}}</ref> which has had over 100,000 copies distributed in its print version as of 2013.

Another of Martin's abiding concerns was the accurate description of the spectrum of atomic [[helium]].  This spectrum is of particular importance as a calibration reference, a benchmark for theoretical calculations of atomic structure and of [[quantum electrodynamics]] effects in atoms, and for applications in astrophysics. Martin's publications on this spectrum, beginning in his early years at NBS and spanning five decades,<ref>{{cite journal|author=Martin, W. C.|year=1959|title=Energy Levels and Spectrum of Neutral Helium (<sup>4</sup>He I)|journal= Journal of Research of the National Bureau of Standards Section A |volume=64|issue=1|pages=19–28|doi=10.6028/jres.064A.003|pmid=32196153|pmc=5287023|doi-access=free}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|author=Martin, W. C.|year=1973|title=Energy Levels of Neutral Helium (<sup>4</sup>He I)|journal=J. Phys. Chem. Ref. Data|volume=2|issue=2|page=257|doi=10.1063/1.3253119|bibcode=1973JPCRD...2..257M|s2cid=98503282}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|author=Martin, W. C.|author2=Sansonetti, Craig J.|year=1983|title=Improved measurement of the <sup>4</sup>He I 3<sup>1</sup>''D'' - 3<sup>3</sup>''D'' separation: Confirmation of predicted mass-polarization isotopic shift|journal=Phys. Rev. A|volume=28|issue=1|page=502|doi=10.1103/PhysRevA.28.502|bibcode=1983PhRvA..28..502M}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|author=Sansonetti, Craig J.|author2=Martin, W. C.|year=1984|title=Accurate wave-number measurements for the <sup>4</sup>He I 1''s''2''p'' - 1''s''3''d'' transitions and comparisons of several term separations with theory|journal=Phys. Rev. A |volume=29|issue=1|page=159|doi=10.1103/PhysRevA.29.159|bibcode=1984PhRvA..29..159S}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|author=Martin, W. C.|year=1984|title=New values for some <sup>4</sup>He I 1''snl'' energy levels, ionization energies, and Lamb shifts|journal=Phys. Rev. A|volume=29|issue=4|page=1883|doi=10.1103/PhysRevA.29.1883|bibcode=1984PhRvA..29.1883M}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|author=Martin, W. C.|year=1987|title=Improved <sup>4</sup>He I 1''snl'' ionization energy, energy levels, and Lamb shifts for 1''sns'' and 1''snp'' terms|url=https://zenodo.org/record/1233705|journal=Phys. Rev. A|volume=36|issue=8|pages=3575–3589|doi=10.1103/PhysRevA.36.3575|pmid=9899293|bibcode=1987PhRvA..36.3575M}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|author=Sims, James S.|author2=Martin, W. C.|year=1988|title= Variational calculations for <sup>4</sup>He I: Improved energies for singlet and triplet ''nD'' and ''nF'' levels (''n'' = 3 - 8)|journal= Phys. Rev. A|volume=37|issue=7|pages=2259–2269|doi=10.1103/PhysRevA.37.2259|pmid=9899927|bibcode=1988PhRvA..37.2259S}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|author1=Drake, W. C.|author2=Martin, W.C.|year=1998|title=Ionization energies and quantum electrodynamic effects in the lower 1''sns'' and 1''snp'' levels of neutral helium (<sup>4</sup>He I)|journal=Can. J. Phys.|volume=76|issue=9|page=679|doi=10.1139/cjp-76-9-679|bibcode=1998CaJPh..76..679D}}</ref> remain the definitive sources of reference data as of 2013.
